en: Imperial Edict on the Implementation of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) by Emperor Taizong Wen of the Tang Dynasty:

The Imperial Decree states: "The Dharma is such that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, because the world has become turbid and frivolous in this final age, he entrusted kings and great ministers with the task of protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma.

Now, as for monks and nuns who have left the household life, their observance of the precepts must be complete. If they indulge their passions in licentiousness, they will encounter affliction at every turn."

This is distressing and involves human affairs; it constantly contravenes the Sūtras and Vinaya. Having lost the profound and subtle intent of the Tathāgata, one also fails in the King’s duty of receiving and upholding the teachings.
The *Śāsanāntara-sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha as he approached his parinirvāṇa to admonish and restrain his disciples;

it is exceedingly detailed and essential. Yet, among the common people and the clergy of this degenerate age, none revere it. The Great Way is about to vanish, and these subtle words are on the verge of being lost forever.

Embracing the Holy Teachings, I intend to propagate and expound them widely. It is fitting that the relevant authorities dispatch ten scribes to transcribe many copies of the scriptures, ensuring they are put into practice as fully as possible.
The necessary paper, brushes, ink, and other supplies shall be provided by the relevant offices.

One copy each shall be presented to officials of the fifth rank and above, as well as to the Prefectural Governors of all provinces. Should you observe the conduct of monks or nuns that does not accord with the scriptural texts...
The same. It is fitting that both the public and private sectors should encourage and exhort one another to ensure its certain observance (from the *Wenguan Cailin*, fascicle 693).
Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty published the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Yijiao jing):
"The Way is not distant from man; the teaching is fundamentally without categories. Although the forms of even the most lowly creatures differ, their desire for eternal bliss is the same."
Their nature is thus identical. It is due to the entanglements of craving and desire that saṃsāra increases.
For this reason, the Sage of Kapilavastu appeared in the world to spread compassion; in the region of Śrāvastī, he expounded the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.

Having encompassed all sentient beings within his salvation, he led them from worldly convention toward the True Reality. Thus, between the twin trees, he universally addressed the assembly of the Mahāyāna, demonstrating—

One may restrain the five faculties, inquire into the doubts regarding the Four Truths, and aspire to the proclamation of the profound Dharma, so as to make the minds of the multitude firm and steadfast;
such is the ultimate expression of the thought of great compassion. I, the Emperor, have reverently succeeded to this auspicious foundation, yet I look upon my own meager virtue with shame.

I have always followed the instructions of my predecessors, hoping thereby to guide others toward the secret exegesis. Having perused this scripture, I have constantly cherished it with reverence and respect, desiring that it be circulated for the benefit of all.

I have therefore had it carved upon wooden printing blocks, in the hope that it may be bequeathed to the various states; may all those within the realm of sentient beings strive together to turn toward it. Thus it is said.
Preface to the Reprinted Commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching):
Within the pure Dharma-realm, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing. Yet, through the power of great compassionate vows, he manifests birth;

within that which is beyond speech, he demonstrates teaching; and within that which is formless, he manifests form. Thus, for forty-nine years, he laid bare the truth, [leaving behind] more than three hundred...
To resolve this entanglement: speaking in general terms, it does not exceed three categories. First is the Sūtra Piṭaka, which elucidates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Thus, in profound stillness and immobility, every dust mote is a pure land of absolute truth; and as the spiritual mirror accords with conditions, in every thought-moment the Buddha-body universally responds.
Second is the Vinaya Piṭaka, which elucidates ethical discipline (*śīla*). Thus, the moment a thought stirs in the mind, every single impulse constitutes a transgression of the *śīlas*.
When one cuts off deliberation and forgets thought, every segment becomes a model of perfection. The third is the Abhidharma Piṭaka (Lun-zang), which elucidates wisdom;
thus it is luminous and not obscure. The myriad stars and constellations are brilliantly arrayed, and the scales, shells, feathers, and fur are clearly visible without being hidden.

Although there are three names, they never possess three distinct essences. Therefore, by examining the guiding lines and rules, the established gates are set forth, thereby threading together the flowers [of the teachings].
He opened the Vinaya-piṭaka and composed his treatises based upon the Upadeśas. Thus, the one is three, and the three are one;
this mutual fusion of the one and the three is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). This present *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* was expounded forty years after [the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa].
Although it is termed a Sūtra, its actual purpose is to re-emphasize the precepts. The World-Honored One, seeing his disciples...
As the *śīla* was about to decline, he addressed the assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa, you should treasure and revere the *prātimokṣa*;
it shall be your Great Teacher. It will be no different from me remaining in the world. You should know that the precepts are the root of right compliance with liberation;
meditative concentration and wisdom arise from them. This is my final instruction as a Buddha. Herein is...

The Buddha’s disciple Gujian Qingming, while lecturing on the transmission [of this text], observed that its commentary was both abridged and its characters so small and blurred that errors such as "three pigs" (sān shǐ) were unavoidable.

He requested that I outline the topical divisions (*gōukē*), supplement the annotations, and revise it for circulation in the world. I do not distinguish between the monastic and the lay; how could I dare to undertake such revision and supplementation?

Yet, as he entreated me again and again, I could not refuse his command and have thus begun. *Note: The "three pigs" (sān shǐ) refers to a famous example from the *Zuozhuan*, where the text "four horses" (sì mǎ) was misread as "three pigs" due to scribal error.*
I have herein set forth its topical outline, briefly supplemented its omissions, corrected its errors and deletions, and recorded the date and month.
Written on an auspicious day in the second lunar month of the year Wanyili Bingxu.

Annotated Commentary on the *Buddha-śāsana-sūtra* by Chan Master Yongxiang Guling Liaotong, a purple-robed śramaṇa specially granted a golden Buddha and jeweled crown by imperial decree to lecture at the Imperial Altar.
Narrated by Guling Liaotong.
The Imperially Appointed Lecturer on the Imperial Altar, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Specially Granted a Golden Buddha and Precious Crown, Chan Master Yongxiang Guling Liaotong’s Supplementary Commentary.
△ Regarding the explanation of this sutra commentary, the structural outline (*pīn*) is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of the title of the sutra.

Within this single title, *The Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra*, there is both person and dharma, and both agent and object. It is titled as such because it combines the person and the dharma, and unites the agent and the object;
thus it is called the *Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra*. This constitutes the general heading. Below, it is explained in detail. "Buddha" (佛) is the Sanskrit term...
It is said that "Buddha" means the Awakened One (*buddha*). This refers to one who has awakened himself, awakened others, and perfected the practice of awakening; thus, he is called a Buddha.
As for "bequeathed" (*yi*), our Great World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, administering the excellent medicine according to the specific ailments of his disciples.
He left this behind for future generations to transform and benefit humans and devas; hence it is called "bequeathed. "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the entire Great Canon.
"Teaching" refers to the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. "Sūtra" is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Scripture of Accordance" (*qijing*).
This means a scripture that accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Thus, the Buddha is the person, and the bequeathed teaching is the Dharma.
The single character "sūtra" (經) refers to the text that expresses; the preceding three characters refer to the meaning expressed.
Thus, both the person and the Dharma are titled together, and the means and the object are combined in the title; hence it is called the *Buddha-śāsana-sūtra* (佛遺教經).
It is titled *The Sutra of Brief Instructions on the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvana*.
This means that the Buddha is the one who enters, and nirvana is that which is entered. Regarding "nirvana": *nie* (ni) means non-arising, and *pan* (vāṇa) means non-ceasing.
Being neither arising nor ceasing, it is the ultimate fruit of true permanence. "Briefly explained" means abbreviated in contrast to an extensive explanation.
As for the "Exhortation": our Great World-Honored One, out of his profound compassion, exhorted us with repeated and earnest instruction.
△ Second, the time of the translator:
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, by imperial decree.
Yao Qin was the ruler of the Eastern Jin dynasty. His surname was Yao and his given name was Xing; he served as the King of Qin. Regarding the "Tripitaka" (Sanzang):

this master’s learning permeated the Tripitaka, and he thoroughly mastered the Five Vehicles. His Way shook both the Chinese and the barbarians, and his fame resounded throughout the court and the countryside.
Therefore, he is given this title. As for the Dharma Master: he is vast and widely learned, capable of upholding all words, phrases, and sentences;
he definitively and well understands the characteristics of arising and ceasing in all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds; and he has attained meditative concentration and wisdom.

One who accords with all the teachings of the sūtras without contention, neither adding to nor diminishing them, but acts according to what has been taught, is therefore called a Dharma Master (*dharmabhāṇaka*).
Furthermore, a Dharma Master bestows the True Dharma (*saddharma*) upon gods and humans, pervading the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust;
thus is he called a Dharma Master. The Sanskrit name Kumārajīva is translated here as "Child-Life" (*Tóngshòu*); this means that although he was a child, [he possessed the life-span of an elder].
There was one of venerable virtue who, having received an imperial edict from the King of Qin, translated this sutra. To translate from Sanskrit (Fan) into Chinese (Hua) is called "yi" (translation).
△ Third, the colophon regarding the title:
Annotated by the śramaṇa Shousui, a successor to the patriarchs at the Lanruo Hermitage on Fengshan in Yunxiao, Song.
Yunjiao refers to Yunyang Prefecture in Huguang. Fengshan is named after its form;
this mountain resembles a phoenix, and it is also the name of the mountain itself. "Aranya" is a Sanskrit term, which here means a place of tranquility.
"Successor to the Patriarch" (Sizu) refers to one who inherits the position of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from his master.

"Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Diligent Quiescence. Because he diligently cultivates precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and extinguishes greed, hatred, and delusion, he is called a Śramaṇa.
"Shangshou Xiasui" is the name of the Master. Regarding "Commentary" (Zhu): it is said that having a presiding authority at the side is called a "Commentary. Furthermore...

To divide the text into sections and analyze the meaning is called a "commentary" (zhù). △ Fourth, the explanation of the main body of the scripture has three parts. First, the introductory section has three parts.
First, the introduction concerning the initial conversion: Śākyamuni Buddha.

In Sanskrit, this is called Śākyamuni. "Śākya" means "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren), referring to one who regards the four modes of birth as his only child, harboring a heart of compassion that identifies with all beings, and observing the three realms with universal benevolence, initiating boundless transformation through great kindness.
"Muni" means "Silent and Still" (Jimo), signifying that its essence is silent and inactive, while its function is numinous and luminous, never obscured. Therefore, he is called "Śākyamuni."
*Kāśyapa-muni*. "Buddha" is one of the ten titles [of a Tathāgata].

The initial turning of the Wheel of Dharma refers to the wheel of the Four Noble Truths turned in three ways. The "three ways" refer to: the turning that demonstrates the characteristics [of the truths], namely: "This is suffering," which oppresses...
This is the nature of compulsion; this is origination. This is the nature of being enticed; this is cessation. This is the nature of being realizable; this is the path.
This is the nature of being cultivatable. Turning toward cultivation: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is origination; you should abandon it. This is cessation."
"You should realize this: 'This is the path. You should cultivate this: 'This is suffering; it has been known by me.
This is its origin; it has been abandoned by me. This is its cessation; it has been realized by me. This is the path; it has been cultivated by me.'"
Having delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya, there were these five men: three from his paternal clan—first Āśvajit, second Bāṣpa, and third Mahānāman.
There were two from the maternal clan: one was Kauṇḍinya and the other was Vīraka-Kāśyapa; together there were five people. "Ājñāta" is the name [of the first];
this translates as "One Who Has Known. It does not mean that he has nothing to know, but rather that he knows "non-existence" (i.e., the cessation of suffering). "Kauṇḍinya" is his family name.
This is called the Fire-Weapon (Agnidatta). His ancestors served fire; from this, the clan was named. △ Second, the conclusion of the sequence:
the final teaching, in which he delivered [the Dharma] to and liberated Subhadra.
Our Great World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years. This was his final instruction as he was about to conclude his profound proclamation.
"Subhadra" is the Sanskrit term; in this [language], it means "One Who Cherishes the Wise. In the language of Tang, it is "Shanxian" (Good Virtue).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Subhadra was intelligent and possessed great wisdom. He recited the four *Veda* scriptures and there was no treatise or book that he did not master."
Dāruka was revered by all people. Upon hearing that the Buddha had entered nirvana, he went to the Buddha’s location;

there, hearing the Eightfold Noble Path, his mind was opened and liberated, and he subsequently attained the first fruit of the path. He then left the household life to become a monk under the Buddha.
Those who were to be delivered have all already been delivered.
Regarding those who were to be delivered, there are also some who were not to be delivered. Why is this? It refers to the fourfold assembly and others.
The causes and conditions having already matured, they realized the fruit upon hearing the Dharma just once; all have now been delivered.
Yet the old woman of the eastern city and others were born in the same place as the Buddha, and the Buddha was unable to transform them into goodness.
△ Third, the manifestation of parinirvāṇa.
Between the twin śāla trees, he was about to enter nirvāṇa.
These trees consisted of four pairs, or eight individual trunks; four were in full bloom while four were withered. The four in bloom symbolized permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The four withered trees symbolize suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence. At the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa, all eight trees turned white;
this is also called the Crane Forest (Kakudha-vana). Regarding the phrase "about to enter nirvana": "about to" (jiāng) means that it has not yet been completed;
it refers to being on the verge of passing into extinction, but not yet having passed into extinction.
At this time, during the middle watch of the night, all was silent and still. For the sake of his disciples, he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma.
He said: "The 'middle watch' symbolizes the wondrous principle of the Middle Way. It is tranquil and unmoving; it is without sound and without form.

Yet, it does not hinder the spontaneous resonance that leads to universal penetration. In transcending the world to deliver sentient beings, there is no condition to which it does not respond. Whether in cessation or non-cessation, both are but skillful means."
The ritual of manifesting extinction is the same for every Buddha. This earnest entrustment expresses the inexhaustibility of their compassionate vows.
In the past, over forty-nine years and more than three hundred assemblies, from the beginning at the Deer Park to the end at the Bāhudā River, the Great Matter was brought to completion.
Herein, he briefly expounds the essential Dharma for the sake of future generations.
This is merely the governing framework. ○ The above concludes the introductory section.

△ Second, the main body of the teaching (the *zhengzongfen*), in nineteen parts. First, the re-exposition of the precepts (*jiefǎ*), in four parts. First, regarding the primary precepts (*chóngjiè*): as a teacher.
"O you bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should revere, treasure, and honor the Prātimokṣa—translated in the Song dynasty as 'Individual Liberation.
It consists of the seven branches of body and speech, each separately preventing what is non-virtuous; this is the full precepts."
Like those who encounter light in the darkness, or a poor man who finds a treasure, you should know that this is your great teacher;
were I to remain in the world, it would be no different than this.
Revere the precepts as you would the Buddha; the Buddha is ever present therein. 2. Regarding wrong livelihood due to the precepts:
Those who uphold the pure precepts must not engage in buying and selling or trade. They must not acquire fields or houses, nor keep people, slaves, or livestock.
All forms of planting and cultivation, as well as various treasures and wealth, should be kept far away from them, just as one avoids a pit of fire.
To seek worldly gain is to add fuel to the fires of karma; to set one's will upon non-action is for the pearl of precepts to transcend all comparison.

One must not cut down grass or trees, nor plow the soil or dig the earth; one must not compound medicinal decoctions, practice divination of good or ill fortune, gaze upward at the constellations, or calculate the waxing and waning of the cycles.
This refers to calculating and measuring the fullness and emptiness of heaven and earth; hence it is called "calculating the fullness and emptiness.
Furthermore, it is said that "calculating" (tui-bu) means examining the geography below, while "fullness and emptiness" (ying-xu) means observing the celestial phenomena above.
All calculations of past kalpas and reckonings are irrelevant here. One should restrain the body, eat at the proper times, and maintain a pure livelihood.

Regarding "tying a goose with grass": there was once a bhikṣu whose wealth was plundered by bandits. He would rather cast away his life than violate his precepts. As for "tying with grass," it refers to that bhikṣu who, when his property was seized by thieves, [chose to die].
He was tied to a blade of grass and did not dare move for several days, fearing he might harm the green grass; hence it is called "tied to grass.

As for the "goose and the pearl": there was once a monk who went to a donor's house to beg for alms. That household possessed a golden pearl, which the monk saw had been swallowed by a goose and lodged in its belly.
When the donor searched for the pearl but could not find it, he saw only the monk and concluded that [the monk must have taken it].

This monk had stolen [the gold]. He was subjected to beatings and abuse that were unbearable. Suddenly, it was reported that the goose had died. The monk said, "Stop for now; do not strike me further.
I saw that the gold and pearls were eaten by the goose and can be recovered. The master said, "Why did you not say so sooner?
The monk replied, "I feared it would harm its life, and therefore I did not dare speak. Now that it has died, I have only just spoken. As it was in ancient times...
It is so. Why is it not so now? The practice of divination regarding fortune and misfortune, the habit of wrong livelihood, and all that is not pure—these must not involve oneself in worldly affairs.

One must not act as a messenger to facilitate missions, nor employ incantations, elixirs, or charms to cultivate intimacy with the noble, nor engage in familiarity or disrespect; none of these should be done.

"Xié" (媟) is pronounced "xiè. "Màn" (嫚) is pronounced "màn. ○ To employ spells and medicines as messengers is to turn one's back on the path of Nirvana; to form noble connections and act with arrogance is to follow the current of birth and death.
One should instead rectify the mind and maintain right mindfulness to seek deliverance.
With a focused mind and right mindfulness, the further shore is not far away.
One must not conceal flaws or manifest extraordinary signs to delude the masses.
Within, one must not hide minor failings but reveal them to renew oneself; without, one must not ostentatiously display what is not genuine to unworthily receive reverence.
He is respectful.
Regarding the four types of offerings, he knows moderation and contentment:
for clothing and bedding, he has nothing beyond what is necessary for his body; regarding food, drink, and medicine, he is content with whatever he receives through alms.
One should obtain provisions for service as needed; one should not hoard them.
One should not accumulate surplus, remaining free from attachments even while traveling or staying abroad. △ Third, the brief exposition of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra.
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts. Since the precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation, they are called *pāramitā*.
The *Prātimokṣa* establishes the summary characteristics of the precepts. Those who uphold them correctly accord with liberation; those who violate them correctly accord with affliction.

Regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, and what constitutes upholding or violating, these are fully detailed in the various Vinaya texts. The Great Sage has provided this brief instruction; one must strive to practice it accordingly. △ Fourth, the Precepts give rise to Concentration and Wisdom.
Relying upon and depending on this precept, one attains the various meditative concentrations as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
For this reason, bhikṣus, you should maintain pure precepts and not allow them to be broken or deficient. If a person can maintain pure precepts, they will be able to possess wholesome dharmas;
if there are no pure precepts, all virtuous merits cannot arise. Therefore, you should know that the precepts are the foremost source of peace and security.
This is the abode of merit.

From precepts arises concentration; from concentration arises wisdom. Within the entirety of the temporal teachings throughout a single lifetime, there is nothing that is not encompassed by these three dharmas.
Sentient beings have been obscured by the heavy barriers of karma and delusion since beginningless ignorance; yet, if they were to fully possess these three dharmas, they should [attain liberation].
The mindfulness [of these] subsides. All wholesome dharmas and merits should be established by means of mindfulness upon this.
△ Second, the careful guarding of the sense-gates, in three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.
"You bhikṣus, having already been able to abide in the precepts, you should now restrain the five faculties so that they do not become lax and enter into the five desires.
(2) Both the Dharma and the parable are explained together.
It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over his herd, not allowing them to run wild and trespass upon the crops.
If one lets the five sense-faculties run loose, they will not stop at mere sensual desires; they will become boundless and impossible to restrain.

The preceding section established precepts based on specific incidents to prevent wrongdoing and cease evil. Now, it clarifies the need for careful guarding of the sense gates, which must always be managed and restrained.
As Mazu asked Shigong, "What do you do for a living? Gong replied, "I herd oxen. Mazu asked, "How do you herd them?
Gong said, "The nose-rope is always in my hand. Whenever one strays into the grass, I grab the nose and pull it back."
The Patriarch said: "So it is, so it is.
It is like a wild horse that, if not controlled by a bridle, will drag its rider and cause them to fall into a pit or a ravine.
(The character *pèi* [pronounced pì] refers to a horse's halter. "The mind-horse is difficult to tame; the precepts serve as its bridle."

To be robbed and harmed causes suffering that lasts but a single lifetime; however, the calamity of the thieves of the five sense-faculties brings disaster upon successive generations. Their harm is exceedingly grave;
one must not fail to be cautious.

Human life and worldly wealth—the suffering they bring lasts only for this present life. But the life of wisdom and the wealth of the Dharma—if one is impoverished of these, the suffering endures for eternal kalpas.
The difference between light and heavy is as vast as heaven and earth; how can one not be cautious?
Therefore, the wise person restrains [the mind] rather than following it, holding it as one would a thief, not allowing it to run wild.

They maintain the mind through right contemplation: that the faculties and their objects are fundamentally empty; since both self and phenomena are thus, how can攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging/conditioning) arise?
Even if you were to let them run wild, they would all soon be seen to perish;
their deluded sentiments are not real and vanish in an instant.
These five faculties have the mind as their master; therefore, you all should skillfully restrain the mind.
The five faculties are illusory, and deluded consciousness acts as their ruler. To restrain this deluded ruler, one must practice both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) together.
The mind is more fearsome than a venomous snake, a ferocious beast, or a vengeful thief; even a raging conflagration is insufficient to serve as a metaphor for its danger.
The worldly poisons and evils that cannot be easily illustrated are such because they can harm the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
It is like a person holding a vessel of honey in their hand who, moving about with haste and instability, looks only at the honey and fails to see the deep pit.
Deluded mind and deluded objects become increasingly firm through attachment; one stirs restlessly within the deep pit of hell without even realizing it.
It is like a mad elephant without a goad or a monkey that has found a tree—leaping, bounding, and scrambling about, difficult to restrain.
One must urgently subdue it and not allow it to become heedless.
The wild elephant of the mind is like a restless monkey; the precepts serve as its hook and chain.
To let this mind run wild is to lose all that is wholesome for humanity; to restrain it in one place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
When not a single thought arises, all conditions are suddenly stilled. △ Third, the summary exhortation to diligent subjugation:
"Therefore, bhikṣu, you should be diligent and energetic; subdue your own mind."
Knowing that the mind is fundamentally empty, one should diligently subdue it; realizing that objects are eternally quiescent, one should practice with tireless vigor.
△ Third, regarding the reception of food, do not increase the four [faults]. First, the actual eating.
"O bhikṣus, when you receive various foods and drinks, you should regard them as taking medicine. Whether they be good or bad, do not give rise to feelings of preference or aversion;
accept whatever is necessary merely to sustain the body and eliminate hunger and thirst."
Medicine is used to treat illness; food is taken to satisfy hunger. One should not give rise to greed for what is pleasant, nor give rise to anger toward what is unpleasant.
It is merely to sustain the body so that one may practice the Way. What more could be added or subtracted from this? △ Second, the explanation by analogy.
It is like a bee gathering from flowers: it takes only the nectar without damaging the color or fragrance.
Although the bee gathers from the flowers, the flowers still bear fruit. △ Third, the application to the Dharma.
The bhikṣu is likewise. He receives offerings from others only to alleviate his own afflictions; he must not seek much, for excessive seeking ruins his wholesome mind.
Excessive seeking causes others to give rise to affliction, and when affliction arises, the wholesome mind recedes and perishes. △ Fourth, the conclusion by means of an analogy.
For example, it is like a wise person who gauges the amount of strength a cow can bear and does not overexert it until its power is exhausted.
One should likewise measure one’s own virtuous conduct and gauge accordingly, guarding the mind against transgressions so that it is never depleted.
△ Fourth, the three points on practicing goodness without losing it: first, practicing day and night.

"You, bhikṣus, should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas during the day so as not to let the time pass in vain. During the first watch and the last watch of the night, you must likewise not neglect them.
During the middle watch, recite the sūtras to allow yourself to rest."

Three times during the day and three times at night, like the tide of the ocean, one should respond without missing the proper time. The first and last watches of the night represent the two extremes;
the middle watch represents the Middle Way. The three contemplations should proceed in succession like a hen brooding her eggs—how could there be a distinction between day and night?
△ Second, the precept against sleep:
Do not allow this life to pass in vain due to the causes and conditions of sleep, resulting in nothing attained.

You should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek liberation for yourself early and do not sleep. The thieves of the various afflictions are constantly watching for an opportunity to kill you.
People are worse than enemies; how can you sleep without awakening yourself?
The venomous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart, like a black viper sleeping in your room. You must use the hook of moral discipline to expel it as soon as possible.
Only when the sleeping snake has been driven out may you sleep in peace; to sleep while it remains is the act of a shameless person.
It shrouds the true nature and increases ignorance; due to the fault of sleep, this is a lack of shame and remorse.
Formerly, Aniruddha was the Buddha’s younger cousin, the son of King Śuklodana. After he had gone forth into the homeless life—
He was excessively fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked him, saying: "Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster;

if you sleep for a thousand years, you shall not hear the name of the Buddha. Having heard the Buddha’s rebuke, he wept and reproached himself, remaining awake for seven days until he lost both his eyes.
The Buddha then instructed him to cultivate the *Ratnaketu-virocana-vajra-samādhi*, whereupon he attained it.
With the divine eye, one knows that the former Buddhas strictly established the precepts, proclaiming them in detail and with repeated emphasis. They spoke with bitter words out of their compassion;
truly, they must not be neglected. △ Third, the conclusion on shame and remorse.
The garment of shame is the foremost among all forms of adornment. Shame is like an iron hook, capable of restraining a person from what is unrighteous.
Therefore, monks, you should always maintain a sense of shame and never allow it to falter for even a moment. If one is devoid of shame, then all virtuous qualities will be lost.
One who possesses a sense of conscience possesses the wholesome Dharma; one who lacks a sense of conscience is no different from the birds and beasts.
It is distinct.
Among the six realms of existence, it is only within the human realm that one can rectify the mind and its deliberations to advance toward Bodhi.

If a person does not do so, they are said to lack a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*). If these two—shame and remorse—are fully possessed, they constitute the raiment of the Dharma-body.
How can one be so shameless and devoid of remorse as to delight in sleep and fail to advance on the Path? "Shame" (hrī) is inward self-reproach;
"remorse" (apatrāpya) is the disclosure of faults to renew oneself. Is this not truly sublime? △ Fifth, the practice of patience surpasses that of morality.
Part One: Enduring Harm Without Anger.
"O bhikṣus, suppose someone were to come and cut you limb from limb.
As the Sūtra says, the Buddha declared: 'In five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of patience;
when King Kali severed my body and cut me limb from limb, if at that time there had been any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span...'"

One would naturally give rise to anger and resentment. At that time, because there is no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span, one does not give rise to anger and resentment.

One should restrain one's own mind so as not to allow anger and resentment to arise; one should also guard one’s speech and refrain from uttering evil words. If one gives rein to a heart of wrath, [it will lead to further suffering].

This will hinder one's own progress on the Path and cause one to lose the benefits of merit. As for the virtue of patience (*kṣānti*), it is something that neither the observance of precepts nor ascetic practices can equal.
One who is able to practice patience may truly be called a powerful person of great stature.
If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of malicious abuse as if drinking ambrosia (*amṛta*), one cannot be called a wise person who has entered the Path.
When wisdom is luminous, then "other" and "self" are not two. When "other" and "self" are not two, then beauty and ugliness cease together.
When beauty and ugliness cease together, then enemies and kin are viewed with equality. When enemies and kin are viewed with equality, then suffering and pleasure have no place to lodge.

Master Fu said: "The patient mind is like an illusion or a dream; the object of insult is like the hair of a tortoise. If one can constantly maintain this contemplation, when encountering difficulties, they will instead—"
"Solid and firm! Truly well said! II. Inquiry and Explanation of Guarding. Why is this so?
The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas and ruins one's good reputation; in both this life and future lives, people will not wish to see such a person.
One should know that a mind of anger is more fierce than a raging fire; one must always guard against it and not allow it to arise.

To enter [the path] and yet harbor anger is to be a thief of merit; nothing surpasses this. A layperson who pursues sensual desires is not a practitioner of the Way and lacks the Dharma to restrain themselves;
in their case, anger may still be excused. But for one who has left the home life to practice the Way—a person free from desire—to harbor anger is utterly unacceptable.

The extensive explanation of the afflictions and harms of anger is as follows: they all arise because of attachment to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), being deluded and failing to know how to turn back.
A single thought of anger gives rise to a million gates of obstruction; it opens up as the root of affliction (*kleśa*) and is the fire of the three miserable realms (*tri-apāya*).
While worldly truths might be excusable, how can a child of the Buddha in the supramundane truth not be cautious? How can one not be cautious? △
Third, the conclusion by means of a dual analogy:
For example, it is as inappropriate as lightning striking and igniting fire within clear, cool clouds.
Observance of the precepts is like ice and frost—pure and untainted; how could the fire of anger, which is like a bolt of lightning, ever be purified?
"Cool. This refers to the fact that water and fire do not occupy the same vessel, and cold and heat do not coexist at the same time. △ Six: Right Livelihood through Begging for Food, in two parts.
First: Holding the Alms Bowl in Accordance with Proper Ritual.
"You, bhikṣus, should stroke your own heads, having abandoned ornaments and finery; wearing robes of dyed color, you should carry alms-bowls and sustain yourselves by begging."
Wearing tattered robes and carrying an alms bowl, one follows the Buddha’s disciplinary code; seeking food to sustain the body is what constitutes right livelihood.
Second, subduing arrogance to enter into the principle:
seeing for oneself in this way, if arrogance should arise, one must swiftly extinguish it. To increase arrogance is not even fit for the mundane world.

This is appropriate even for laypeople in white robes; how much more so for those who have left the household life to enter the Way? For the sake of liberation, they humble themselves and go forth to beg.
Thus they subdue arrogance, enter the family of the Tathāgata, and with body and mind made lowly, they accord with the principle of liberation. △ Seven: Directness.
Regarding the two ways of practicing the Path with the mind: first, both the crooked and the straight are explained together.
"O bhikṣus, a crooked and deceitful mind is contrary to the Path; therefore, you should make your minds upright and sincere."
You should know that deceit and crookedness serve only to deceive; for those who have entered the Path, such things have no place.
Second, concluding that integrity is the foundation:
Therefore, you all should rectify your minds and take straightforwardness as your fundamental principle.
Deceitfulness and crookedness abound in fraud; a straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). △ Section Eight: Attaining Success through Few Desires. Part One:
Explaining Both Excess and Moderation.
"You bhikṣus, you should know that because those with many desires seek many gains, their suffering and affliction are likewise many. Those with few desires..."
Such a person has no seeking and no desire; thus, they have no such affliction.
All seeking is suffering; if there is no desire, what worry can there be? △ Second, the benefits of having few desires.
Even mere fewness of desire (*alpecchatā*) should be cultivated; how much more so since fewness of desire can give rise to all manner of meritorious qualities.
A person of few desires has no crookedness or flattery to seek the favor of others, nor are they led astray by the sensory faculties (*indriya*).
One who practices fewness of desire has a mind that is level and serene, free from anxiety or fear; in all matters they have abundance and are never lacking. To possess few desires—
If one possesses this, then there is *nirvāṇa*. This is called having few desires (*alpeccha*).
Such is the merit of the single dharma of having few desires. Merely practicing having few desires has such merit;
it is still worth cultivating, let alone when it is conjoined with liberation and *nirvāṇa*. △ Ninth: Contentment and Pure Joy. Part Two: First, Liberation.
Having undergone suffering, you have now attained peace. You bhikṣus, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering and affliction, you should contemplate contentment.
The dharma of contentment is itself the place of wealth, joy, and security.
△ Second, the mutual clarification of sufficiency and insufficiency:
A person who knows contentment is peaceful and happy even when lying upon the bare ground; one who lacks contentment, though dwelling in heaven, is not so.
Nor does it accord with one's wishes. One who lacks contentment is poor despite being wealthy; one who possesses contentment is rich despite being poor.
One who lacks contentment is constantly led astray by the five desires and is pitied by those who possess contentment. This is called contentment.

Contentment causes the mind to cease its longing; one possesses pure joy in abundance. For those who lack contentment, craving increases ever further, and the wheel of suffering is difficult to still.
△ Ten: Tranquility and Detachment from the Multitude, Part Three. First: The Place of Stillness is Admired by the Heavens.
"You bhikṣus, if you wish to seek the peace of the unconditioned and dwell in bliss, you should leave behind clamor and bustle, dwelling alone in seclusion.
(Kòng, from the *gǔ* rhyme group; *nào*, from the *nú* rhyme group. When mind and objects are tranquil and still, one becomes solitary and upright."
Those who dwell in solitude are held in common reverence by Śakra and the various devas;
like the Venerable Subhūti, who sat in meditative seclusion among the crags while Śakra and the devas rained down flowers—such instances of his deeds are numerous.
△ Second, both the teaching and the analogy are clarified together.
Therefore, one should abandon one's own group and others' groups;
one should abandon all followers, both one's own and those of others.
Dwelling alone in seclusion, one contemplates the eradication of the root of suffering and abides peacefully in nirvana.
If one delights in crowds, one will undergo manifold afflictions; it is like a great tree: when flocks of birds gather upon it, it becomes withered and broken.
...the affliction of worldly bondage and attachment, sinking into manifold suffering.
Regarding the term "multitude" (*gaṇa*), there are two meanings in terms of both phenomenon (*vastu*) and principle (*artha*). As for the phenomenon, it refers to clamor and bustle.

As for the principle, some take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to be the multitude, while others take all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be the multitude. Being deludedly attached to the five aggregates and accumulating afflictions, one sinks into [suffering].
Because of birth and death, one must distance oneself from views of body and mind. Yongjia said:
"If you see the mountains and forget the Way, then the myriad phenomena will dazzle your eyes and sounds will deafen your ears; though you dwell alone in mountain forests, how can there be stillness?

If you see the Way and forget the mountains, then amidst city walls and bustling markets, the mind and its objects are serene; the ten thousand dharmas are fundamentally at ease, yet it is people themselves who [create distraction]."

Noisy! Turn the light back to reflect upon itself; wherever it touches, it is that very source. There is not a single dharma that can confront the mind, nor is there a single dharma that can accommodate the mind.
To attain this state where nothing is to be abandoned is simply to eliminate all illusions. △ Third, the summary using a single metaphor.
For example, it is like an old elephant mired in mud, unable to extricate itself; this is called "separation.
Attachment to the company of others is a burden; one should cultivate the practice of separation. △ Eleven: Diligent Practice Without Sloth (in two parts).
First, the Dharma and Simile of Diligent Practice.
"O bhikṣus, if you are diligent and energetic, then there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
By practicing with diligence, the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected.
Therefore, you should all be diligent and energetic. It is like a small stream of water: if it flows constantly, it can pierce through rock."
△ Second, the teaching on the analogy of indolence:

If the practitioner’s mind repeatedly becomes indolent and desists, it is like drilling for fire; if one stops before the heat has generated, although one wishes to obtain fire, the fire will be difficult to find. This is called diligence.
The fire-nature within wood is the direct cause of fire; yet if one does not apply effort and rely upon conditions, the fire will ultimately be difficult to obtain.

If one applies effort without ceasing—just as the nature of water is soft and yielding—it will eventually reach the point of piercing stone. This serves as a metaphor for how gain and loss result from diligence and negligence respectively;
one should therefore exert oneself with vigor. △ Section Twelve: Dispelling Demons through Right Mindfulness (three parts). First, the correct...
"Be mindful of expelling the thieves.
You, bhikṣus, in seeking a virtuous friend, seeking virtuous protection and assistance, there is nothing like unforgetting mindfulness.
This unforgetting mindfulness serves as the support for right concentration. Now, afflictions arise from deluded sentiments; one must observe the principles of the Dharma."
One dispels [distractions] by means of this. When first practicing contemplation, the principle is not yet clearly perceived and the mind does not abide in that principle;

it is necessary to employ the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*) before one can attain contemplation. Mindfulness functions through non-forgetfulness: one correctly directs the mind toward the Dharma and examines its qualities of good and evil.
That which is good is increased and not extinguished; that which is evil is extinguished and not allowed to arise.
If there is one who possesses non-forgetful mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions cannot enter.
With right mindfulness remaining unforgetting, the afflictions do not arise. △ Second, the admonition not to lose it.
Therefore, you should always maintain mindfulness within your hearts. If you lose mindfulness, you will lose all meritorious virtues;
if the power of your mindfulness is firm and strong, even if you enter among the thieves of the five desires, you will not be harmed by them.
If the internal is unmoving, the external cannot disturb it. △ Third, the conclusion by means of a simile:
It is like donning armor and entering the ranks; then one has nothing to fear. This is called "unfailing mindfulness."
With right mindfulness ever present, the armies of Māra will be utterly destroyed. △ Thirteen: Controlling the Mind to Know Illusion. Part One: Concentrating the Mind to Know Cessation.
"You bhikṣus, if you control the mind, the mind will abide in samādhi. Because the mind abides in samādhi, one is able to know the world."

The characteristics of arising and ceasing are stilled within the pure, translucent water of meditative concentration, where the myriad phenomena of the universe appear as reflections. △ Second, the admonition against distraction:
For this reason, monks, you should always cultivate various forms of meditative concentration with diligent perseverance.
Whether shallow or deep, all the various samādhis, both great and small, should be cultivated.
If one attains samādhi, the mind will not be distracted;
as distraction gradually ceases, one accords with the gateways of concentration. △ Third, the dual conclusion through both dharma and analogy.

For example, just as a household that cherishes water carefully maintains its dikes and ponds, so too does the practitioner, for the sake of the water of wisdom, skillfully cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) so that it does not leak away; this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
If one lacks the power of concentration (*samādhi*), dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) cannot escape the wheel of suffering. Because concentration can support wisdom, an ancient said:
"The Bodhisattva’s cool moon constantly traverses ultimate emptiness; when the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within it.
If the water is turbid or the vessel is broken, then the lunar reflection will not appear. △ Fourteen: Wisdom Eliminates Afflictions (Part 4). First.
"By abandoning greed, one attains liberation.
You bhikṣus, if you possess wisdom, you will have no greedy attachment; always examine yourselves so as not to fall into error."
Wisdom is the precursor; it must not be lacking for even a moment.
Only thus can one attain liberation within my Dharma.
To lack wisdom is called bondage; to possess wisdom is called liberation. Second, both names [of bondage and liberation] are lost.
If it were not so, one would be neither a person of the Way nor a layperson; there would be no name for such a person.
The mind and the body would be at odds, and both titles would be lost. △ Third, the benefits of wisdom.
True wisdom is a sturdy vessel for crossing the ocean of old age, sickness, and death.
The true wisdom of *prajñā* can cross the sea of suffering;
it is also the great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance.
The great night of ignorance is illuminated by the lamp of wisdom;
it is the excellent medicine for all who are ill.
The grave disease of the three poisons is cured by wisdom.
It is the sharp axe for felling the tree of afflictions.
The roots and stumps of affliction can be cut down by the blade of wisdom;
therefore, you all should augment yourselves through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one gradually increases [one's realization] and enters samādhi. △ Fourth, the summary that establishes wisdom:
If a person possesses the illumination of wisdom, although they have only physical eyes, they are one who sees clearly; this is what constitutes wisdom.
The physical eye shines forth universally; ignorance is forever extinguished—this is the power of wisdom. Therefore, he is called a person of clear vision.
△ Fifteen. Discursive Elaboration Hinders the Path. Part One: The Statement.
"O bhikṣus, if you engage in various forms of conceptual proliferation, your minds will become distracted. Although you have left the household life, you have still not attained liberation.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or staying still, if you deviate from the proper rules of conduct, it will cause the mind to become disordered and contravene the principle of liberation. △ Second, the conclusion.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should swiftly abandon the distracted mind and frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
If you desire to attain the bliss of tranquility (*śānti*), you must only skillfully extinguish the affliction of frivolous proliferation; this is called "non-proliferation."
If one extinguishes frivolous discourse and false conceptualization, the bliss of nirvana may be approximated. △ Section Sixteen:
Settling the Mind and Dispelling Indolence (3). Part One: Admonishing Against Associating with Enemies.
"You, bhikṣus, should always be single-minded regarding all meritorious qualities; you must abandon all negligence and dissolute extravagance as if fleeing from enemies and thieves.
All that was spoken for your benefit by the World-Honored One of Great Compassion has now reached its ultimate conclusion."
△ Second, the exhortation to practice diligently:
"You should simply practice this with diligence.
Through the skillful means of great compassion, I have distinguished and taught three [vehicles]; yet ultimate nirvana is the single path of the One Vehicle."
Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, at the foot of a tree, in a secluded place, or in a quiet chamber, one should recollect the teachings received and,
according to one's capacity, reflect upon and cultivate them.
Do not allow it to be forgotten or lost. You should always exert yourself and cultivate this with diligence.
Strive with earnest application to prevent decline or loss.
Do not die in vain, lest you later come to regret it.
Wandering through the cycle of birth and death—what benefit is there in regret? △ Third, the conclusion by means of two analogies:
"I am like a skilled physician who diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether it is taken or not is not the fault of the physician."
The Buddha preaches the medicine of the Dharma to cure the disease of afflictions; if one hears it and yet does not believe or take it, this is not the fault of the Buddha.
It is like a skillful guide who leads people onto the good path; if they hear it and do not act upon it, this is not the fault of the guide.
The Buddha is the Great Guide who leads sentient beings to the right path of Nirvana. If they do not believe or practice, whose fault is it?
△ Seventeenth: A Repeated Question Warning Against Doubt.
If you have any doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the others, you may ask about them quickly;
do not harbor uncertainty without seeking a resolution.
Within these teachings of the Four Noble Truths, whatever you doubt and have not yet resolved, I shall resolve for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One made this proclamation three times, yet no one questioned him;
the assembly remained silent and did not inquire. Why was this so?
This is an inquiry, for there is no doubt among the assembly.
This explains the meaning of not asking further. △ Eighteen: Substituting and Expanding upon the Three [Truths]. First: The Four Truths are Unchanging.
At that time, Aniruddha— *āniruddha* (the *nu* in *āniruddha* is pronounced with a level tone)—

whose Sanskrit pronunciation differs slightly from the Chinese transliteration, and whom the Song dynasty referred to as "The Undying" (*wúmiè*)— observed the minds of the assembly. Using his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*),
he examined the intentions of the multitude.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the moon might be made hot, and the sun might be made cold; but that which the Buddha has taught regarding the Four Noble Truths cannot be otherwise.
The natures of water and fire might be made indeterminate, but the words of the Buddha are true and certainly not false."
The Buddha taught that the truth of suffering is truly suffering; it cannot be made into pleasure.
Suffering is the fruit of worldly existence; as a truth, it is to be examined and verified, for it is definitively without pleasure.
Accumulation is truly the cause; there is no other cause.
Accumulation (*samudaya*) is the worldly cause; it is the accumulation of all unwholesome karmas. Determination (*niyama*) is the cause that brings about suffering.
If suffering is extinguished, then its cause is extinguished.
The cause of all suffering is rooted in craving. If craving is extinguished, there is nothing for it to depend upon;
because the cause is extinguished, the effect is extinguished. This path to the extinction of suffering is the true path, and there is no other path.
The Truth of Cessation is the supramundane true fruit, which is Nirvana itself. The Truth of the Path is the supramundane true cause for abandoning afflictions; there is no other path.
World-Honored One, these bhikṣus have attained certainty and are free from doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths.
△ Second, the inequality of the two faculties.
Within this assembly, those who have not yet accomplished their task will feel grief and sorrow upon seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
they have not yet realized the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and do not understand that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
If there are those who have newly entered the Dharma, upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, they shall all attain deliverance.
Having personally heard the Buddha’s instructions, there are none who do not receive benefit.
It is like seeing the path immediately when a flash of lightning appears in the night.
For a time, their minds were opened, yet they were not yet able to reach the ultimate goal.
But those who had already accomplished what was to be done and had crossed over the ocean of suffering merely thought: "How swift is the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!"
Although he himself had already attained liberation, out of compassion for those who had not yet crossed over, he gave rise to a thought and uttered a sigh.
△ Third, the conclusion by the Sūtra compiler: Although Ānanda had spoken these words, everyone in the assembly had fully realized the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
Desiring to cause this great multitude to attain firm stability, the World-Honored One, with a heart of great compassion, spoke again for the sake of the assembly.

Those who have not yet attained penetration or completion may, upon hearing of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, experience a decline or fall back. Therefore, at the very end, [the Buddha] earnestly and compassionately offered consolation and encouragement.
△ Nineteen: Admonishing and Exhorting Not to Mourn. Part One: Birth is Inevitably Followed by Extinction.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress. Even if I were to remain in the world for an eon, this assembly would still eventually pass away.
Where there is meeting, separation is inevitable; it can never be avoided."
The law of dependent origination cannot, indeed, be retained. △ Second, both self-benefit and benefiting others are fully realized.
Self-benefit and the benefit of others are both complete within this Dharma.

One accumulates the ten thousand practices and perfects the ten thousand virtues; one expounds the ocean of teachings to benefit all capacities. Thus, the way of universal salvation is entirely present.
If I were to remain for a long time, it would be of no further benefit.

Should the Buddha remain for too long, sentient beings would not conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter; they would fail to plant roots of goodness and become greedily attached to the five desires.
He did not seek to escape from suffering; therefore, the Buddha manifested his parinirvāṇa.
Those who were to be delivered—whether in the heavens or among humans—have all been delivered.
For forty-nine years since attaining the Way, those who were to be delivered have been delivered completely, with none remaining.
As for those who have not yet crossed over, they have all already established the causes and conditions for crossing over.
The pure Dharma-eye and the treasury of precepts, concentration, and wisdom are entrusted internally to Mahākāśyapa and the great disciples,
and externally to kings and ministers, so that the life-force of wisdom may not be severed, serving as the cause and condition for their crossing over.
Listen. △ Above, the section on the True Teaching (Zhengzongfen) is concluded.

△ Third, the section on the Propagation of the Teaching (Liutongfen) has two parts. First, the entrustment for propagation (Zhulailiutong) has five parts. First, the continuous transmission without ceasing.
"From this day forward, my disciples shall transmit and practice this in succession; thus the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata will be eternally present and never extinguished.
The World-Honored One thus entrusted [the teaching], saying that if it is practiced without interruption, the Dharma-body will remain forever. △ Second, praising its rarity in the world.

It is impermanent. Therefore, you should know that the world is entirely impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be separation. Do not harbor grief or distress. Such is the nature of the world:

it is called "the world" (*loka*) because it migrates and flows without staying still; it is called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) because its forms and substances can be described. Since it must meet and manifest birth, how could it be without cessation?
Indeed. △ Third, to incinerate illusions with wisdom:
one should diligently apply effort and seek liberation early. By means of the light of wisdom, extinguish all the darkness of delusion.
Through diligent effort, wisdom becomes clear; when the darkness of delusion is extinguished, one is liberated from all suffering.
The world is truly precarious and fragile; nothing within it is solid or enduring.
(The character for "fragile" is pronounced cuì. Conditioned phenomena are illusory and false, remaining so from the past until now. △ Fourth, showing the extinction that eliminates evil.

I have now attained extinction, like the removal of a malignant disease. This is a sinful thing that ought to be abandoned, falsely named a "body," submerged in the great ocean of old age, sickness, birth, and death.

The Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet he manifests as if it were conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) in order to cause sentient beings to recognize the faults and afflictions of the physical body and to awaken early to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
△ Fifth, concluding with the joy of the wise.
How could a wise person fail to eliminate it, as one would slay a hostile thief, without feeling joy?
The body is the root of suffering and the basis for all miseries; sentient beings delusively cling to it as real and do not seek liberation.
The Great Sage knows that birth and death are all illusory; he manifests birth and death to transform sentient beings. △ Second, the exhortation to circulate [the teaching] has two parts.
"First, diligence brings about the transcendence of impermanence.
You bhikṣus, you should always with a single mind diligently seek the path to liberation and the true path to nirvāṇa."
All phenomena in the world, whether mobile or immobile, are characterized by decay and instability.

The six heavens of the desire realm are mobile phenomena; the two realms of form and formlessness possess long lifespans measured in kalpas, which non-Buddhists reckon as permanent, thus naming them immobile phenomena. II. Admonition to Cease and Follow the Model.
"Cease, all of you; do not speak further. The time is drawing near; I am about to enter parinirvāṇa. This is my final instruction.
Since the proper occasion has arrived, how could I remain much longer? This final model for future guidance is now entrusted to you. Thus he displayed the manner of his transformation.

[This is] a fascicle. It is said that the [deluded] mind has vanished into the profound darkness; yet within the gates of skillful means (*upāya*), how could there not be a pointing and directing? At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Golden Mouth personally proclaimed:
"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I manifest nirvāṇa through skillful means," as is extensively detailed in the "Life Span" chapter (*Tathāgatāyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
Those who know this will find that the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly undispersed. Is this not truly admirable? If one were to say...
Not so. Truly, this is not my way. Why? "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
*The Commentary on the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* (End).
I have once examined the *Chuan deng shi pu* (Lamp Transmission Genealogy), which records that the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and the *Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching*,
annotated by Chan Master Shousui— the thirteenth patriarch of the Caodong school under Qingyuan in the lineage of Dajian— were both collated and revised by Chan Master Liaotong. I...
The printing blocks were carved by the Empress Dowager Cisheng Xuanchenming Su at Yongxiang Temple, located south of Xizhimen Gate in Jintai.
At that time, there was Liu Zaisi, whose courtesy name was Guanzai and sobriquet Niansong; he was a high disciple of the Great Master Yunqi Lianchi.
He upheld the teachings by reciting the Buddha’s name and practiced filial piety and righteousness with sincerity. He served in office as an official of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.

On the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Chongzhen era (the Xinwei year), while traveling by boat to Dongchang, I borrowed the annotated version of the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* from the collection of Dharma Master Zhenyu at Yiwwei Chan Monastery. I transcribed it by hand and brought it back with me.

On the eighth day of the tenth month of the ninth year of the Chongzhen era (the Bingzi year), I borrowed a copy of the *Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra* from the collection of the lay practitioner Shen Guangguan of this locality.
I transcribed it by hand once again, so that it might be joined with the version copied in Dongchang to form a complete set.
He presented it to me with great joy; as I held and read the words of the commentary, they were direct and manifest, like the Buddha’s own injunctions. Its correctness was evident.
Compared with the Yunqi edition, the text contains many differences in wording and phrasing, yet its meaning is truly superior. This recalls Master Lien’s colophon, which states:
"These two sutras are indeed excellent medicines for curing the maladies of the Dharma-ending age;
one is the very first instance of the holy teachings flowing into Zhendan (China). Now, because their language is simple, monks do not recite them, and masters do not lecture upon them. Indeed.
It is not that [the truth] is not exclusively near; there are those who are distant, yet people themselves fail to examine this.
First, this is the final essential teaching of the Tathāgata’s entry into *parinirvāṇa*, comparable to what the world calls a "testament.

For descendants to be ignorant of the origins and sources established by their ancestors is to forget one's root. For descendants to turn their backs on the testament of their parents is to be unfilial. Thus it is said.
"Seng" is the Hu (Sanskrit) word for "not forgetting. This work, along with its verses, was composed by Nian Songshou, who is over sixty years of age.

He has personally transcribed it with a sincere heart and wishes to have it engraved once more to propagate its transmission. It truly and well expresses the aspirations of Master Lian. I, too, wish to lend a hand to bring this project to fruition;
how could I dare claim to be merely contributing according to my limited capacity? Furthermore, I record these words for the sake of all virtuous knowers.
This *vijñāna* (consciousness) successively exhorts and inspires the dependent origination; it is hereby announced to all who see and hear it. May you not treat this with negligence.
Written respectfully by the disciple Tongdeng on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era.
